title: A town of many currents: Hasidim, Mitnagdim, and religious leadership in Drohitchin
summary: The memorial book emphasizes both a largely Mitnagdim community and a Hasidic minority, alongside rabbis and disputes that shaped communal religious life.

editorialConnections.recordTitle: Establishment of a permanent Hasidic prayer house
Destruction and burning of the Hasidic chapter

editorialContent:
## A majority, and a minority with its own place

Drohitchin’s religious life was not a single, uniform tradition. The memorial book describes the [Drohiczyn Jewish community](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_b689953e52a7cfbbe5fa94d4) as mostly Mitnagdim—Jews outside the Hasidic movement—with a smaller Hasidic minority. That distinction shaped the town’s religious landscape, but it did not divide it into two sealed communities. People prayed in different settings, followed different spiritual authorities, and still belonged to the same town.

The memorial book’s editors make a point of explaining why the Hasidim received a dedicated section: Zalman Shevinsky, who wrote it, had been raised in the Hasidic spirit and believed that a small community could be significant beyond its numbers. In his account, Drohitchin’s Hasidim were specifically connected to the [Kobriner dynasty](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_f262be8ffdda22d1cfdf6163), whose rebbes served as spiritual guides for local followers. The book’s description of this minority as small but important is a judgment about its place in communal memory, not a numerical estimate.

The wider record helps locate the town without making its religious balance more exact than the evidence allows. A local history page identifies Drohitchin with several spellings—Drogicin, Drohitchin, and Drahichyn—and places it in the Polesye region. It also describes a long religious life, including a reputation for Kabbalah and the presence of Hasidism. That page is a later compilation, however, and does not independently verify the book’s estimate of the balance between Mitnagdim and Hasidim. ([JewishGen KehilaLinks: Drogicin](https://kehilalinks.jewishgen.org/drogicin/drogicin.html))

## A prayer house for Kobriner Hasidim

A small minority needed somewhere to pray. The book names Nahum Shevinsky as the person who initiated the [permanent Hasidic prayer house](/communities/drohiczyn/records/event_candidate_942b7d82c02167130b2c0b4c) for the local Kobriner Hasidim, after a period when they lacked a dedicated place. The [Hasidic shtibl](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_114773e1eda8f096d109da96) was more than a room for daily prayer: it gave a small group a recognizable communal home and connected local worship to a Hasidic spiritual lineage beyond Drohitchin.

The book’s accounts preserve an uncertainty about the building’s fate. One record describes the [Hasidic chapter](/communities/drohiczyn/records/event_candidate_6cb4da03f5559df303059892) as unfinished and later destroyed and burned; another says the shtibl survived wartime burning intact. These statements may refer to different structures or different moments, but the records provided do not resolve the question. It would be misleading to merge them into a single definitive story of the building.

The Kobriner connection also makes clear that Hasidic life in Drohitchin was not simply a local style of worship. Its adherents looked to the [Kobriner rabbis](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_0c34ef6a730856d03e64e5d4) as guides, linking a small-town prayer house to a wider religious network. A useful next question is whether local records or family papers identify the shtibl’s location: [the Hasidic shtibl’s address](research:Where in Drohitchin was the Kobriner Hasidic shtibl located?).

## Rabbis, succession, and communal authority

Alongside the Hasidic leaders stood rabbis whose authority reached across the town. The memorial book remembers [Davidl Yaffe](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_1a6f71a960648285cc26b8ef) as a rabbinical judge, sage, and Kabbalist, and names [Rabbi Tzvi Eliyahu](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_7cbfce2f350cf5a4ef7ffe60) as a former rabbi whose death prompted a succession dispute. The book’s wider rabbinic narrative traces leadership through Tzvi Eliyahu to his son, [Rabbi Menakhem Reikhman](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_fd1657766b8ed41bca3466b6), and then to Menakhem’s son-in-law, Rabbi Yitsik Yaakov Kalenkavitch. It identifies [Dov Warshawsky](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_29330376a79dda33c00558bf) as the town’s last rabbi.

The JewishGen translation of the memorial book adds a vivid account of an earlier succession conflict: Rabbi Yisrael Valevelsky returned to Drohitchin after the community had appointed Tzvi Eliyahu. The dispute became heated, and a rabbinical court led by the Slonim rabbi, Eisel Kharif, was asked to decide who should serve. The two rabbis agreed to answer questions on Talmud; the account says Tzvi Eliyahu prevailed, and Valevelsky left for Yanova. Later, Menakhem succeeded his father, and Kalenkavitch followed his father-in-law. The same book translation says Menakhem served for about forty years before moving to Palestine, while another passage dates Kalenkavitch’s official appointment to 1903. These details are the memorial book’s testimony, not independent confirmation. ([Memorial book, in JewishGen’s translation](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/drohichyn/dro121.html); [biography of Kalenkavitch](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/drohichyn/dro123.html))

The book also shows that religious authority did not belong to one office alone. It names the Chevra Kadisha, the burial society, among the town’s institutions, and records scholars and religious teachers beyond the chief rabbinate. Rabbis served a shared community even as competing traditions and personal loyalties could make appointments contentious. The succession dispute was therefore not merely a contest between individuals: it concerned who could represent the town’s religious needs and command its confidence.

## Coexistence, tension, and the record’s limits

The strongest evidence of tension in these accounts concerns rabbinic succession; the evidence about everyday relations between Hasidim and Mitnagdim is thinner. The book presents the Hasidim as a minority with a distinct prayer house and spiritual leadership, but it does not describe a sustained conflict between the two groups. Separate institutions could mark difference without proving hostility. The surviving account offers glimpses of overlapping communal life, not a complete map of private loyalties or daily encounters.

Independent sources add context, but they do not settle the religious story. Yad Vashem’s encyclopedia of ghettos describes Drohitchin between the wars as having roughly 1,500 Jewish residents and records its communal institutions, including a Talmud Torah, a Hebrew school, a library, and other cultural activity. It is useful evidence for the breadth of Jewish communal life, but it does not provide an account of the Hasidic–Mitnagdim balance or verify the rabbinic succession in the memorial book. ([Yad Vashem, “Drohiczyn”](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=257))

The same source documents the destruction of the community under German occupation: the killing of Jews in July 1942 and the murder of most of those remaining in October. These events frame what the memorial book could preserve. Its testimony gives names, affiliations, stories, and disputed memories from a community largely destroyed; the archival record supplies a different kind of evidence, especially about persecution and the final years. Neither should be made to speak for the other.

A comparison with neighbouring towns would require more than assuming that Drohitchin’s pattern was typical. Communities could have different numbers of prayer houses, rabbis, and Hasidic followers, and the records consulted here do not establish a systematic regional comparison. What they do show is a town whose religious life held several currents at once: a largely Mitnagdic public, a smaller Kobriner Hasidic group with its own shtibl, and rabbinic lineages whose authority was both inherited and contested. The evidence leaves further questions open, including the identity and role of the [Kobriner Hasidim’s local leaders](research:Which Kobriner rebbe or emissary guided Drohitchin’s Hasidim?) and how worshippers moved between the town’s religious institutions.
